title: 6.8.12 Plain English to Pseudocode: The Slingshot
description: Turn the plain-English rules of a slingshot into pseudocode: grab, stretch and release, guarded by one variable, with the force applied in exactly one frame.

steps.title: Turn the plain-English steps into pseudocode
steps.instructions:
Here is the plan in plain English:

**1.** Each frame, ask three questions in a row.

**2.** Grab: if the mouse was just pressed while over the ball, the ball is now held.

**3.** Stretch: if the ball is held and the mouse is still down, move the ball to the mouse and draw the band.

**4.** Release: if the ball is held and the mouse was let go, work out the force, apply it to the ball, and the ball is no longer held.

**5.** If nothing is being done to the ball (idle), all three answers are no and the frame just ends.

The same plan is drawn as a flow chart above the editor. You do not draw it, you read it: follow the arrows and match each box to one of the steps.

In `README.md`, type these as numbered pseudocode **between the first and last line**. Write three separate IF blocks, one per question, each closed with END IF. Number every line, including the indented ones and the END IF lines. Each keyword looks like this:

- `IF mouse presses AND ball is hovered` ... `END IF` (a question the frame asks)
- `SET held TO true` (a change)
- `CALL drawBand` (call another function)
- `SET ball position TO the mouse` (a change)

The force is applied on exactly **one** frame of the whole throw. If you put `applyForce` on the stretch path, the ball would speed up every frame you hold it.
hints: `held` guards both the stretch and the release. Without it, the release would fire whether or not anything had been picked up.
CALL applyForce goes in the release block only, once.

requirements.title: Ten or more numbered steps in a row
requirements.description: Number every line 1. 2. 3. and so on, with something written after each number.
requirements.hint: You need at least ten lines that start with a number, one after another. Number the indented lines and the END IF lines too.

requirements.title: Grab: press on the ball sets held
requirements.description: An IF about the mouse being pressed on the ball, with SET held TO true inside.
requirements.hint: Grab: IF the mouse presses and the ball is hovered, then SET held TO true, then END IF.

requirements.title: Stretch: held and pressing moves the ball and draws the band
requirements.description: An IF held AND pressing, with the ball moved to the mouse and CALL drawBand inside.
requirements.hint: Stretch: IF held AND mouse is pressing, then move the ball to the mouse and CALL drawBand, then END IF.

requirements.title: Release: held and released applies the force and clears held
requirements.description: An IF held AND released, with CALL applyForce and SET held TO false inside.
requirements.hint: Release: IF held AND mouse is released, then CALL applyForce and SET held TO false, then END IF.

requirements.title: applyForce is called once
requirements.description: One CALL applyForce in the whole plan. A force every frame is the classic physics bug.
requirements.hint: Call applyForce exactly once, in the release block. Not on the stretch path.

requirements.title: Three questions, each closed
requirements.description: Three IF blocks, each closed with END IF.
requirements.hint: Write three IF blocks, each closed with END IF. Do not write GO TO or LOOP BACK.

planChart.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A([draw runs]) --> B{pressed on the ball}
  B -- yes --> C[held = true]
  C --> D{held and pressing}
  B -- no --> D
  D -- yes --> E[move ball to mouse]
  E --> F[[drawBand]]
  F --> G{held and released}
  D -- no --> G
  G -- yes --> H[work out the force]
  H --> I[[applyForce]]
  I --> J[held = false]
  J --> Z([end of frame])
  G -- no --> Z
planChart.caption: One frame of draw(): three questions. The applyForce call sits on a path taken in exactly one frame of the throw.
